subjects.name: The Science of the Heart: Sufi Psychology and the Classical Islamic Inner Life
subjects.description: A close reading of classical and modern Sufi texts on the soul, the ego, divine love, and the disciplines of purification.
subjects.why_this_library: It holds primary texts (al-Ghazali, al-Jilani, Ibn ʿArabi, Ibn ʿAta' Allah) alongside their best modern interpreters (Chittick, Schimmel, Nasr), which almost no general collection does.
subjects.shape: This is a genuinely teachable library built around classical primary texts in translation: two books of Ghazali's Ihya on love and on disciplining the soul, Ibn 'Ata' Allah's Hikam with commentary, Jilani's discourses and Sirr al-Asrar, Nabulusi on seclusion, and Shabrawi on the soul's degrees — enough to run several weeks on nafs, character training, and the stations of the wayfarer straight from the sources. A second strong wing is Rumi and mystical poetics (Chittick's thematic anthology, Schimmel's Rumi's World and As Through a Veil, Rifai's Mathnawi commentary, Sis's Attar), and a third is the speculative/metaphysical register via Nasr and Chittick's two Ibn al-'Arabi volumes. Modern reframings (Frager's Sufi psychology, Bakhtiar's enneagram, Helwa) give a contemporary-reception unit, though the Ibn al-'Arabi and modern-psychology shelves are largely unread.
subjects.holes: The formative period is missing almost entirely: no Qushayri's Risala, no Muhasibi, Sarraj, Kalabadhi, or Sulami — so the course starts at Ghazali with no view of how the vocabulary of nafs, qalb, ruh, and maqamat was built in the 9th-10th centuries. Ibn al-'Arabi is present only through Chittick's exposition, never in direct translation, and there is no Shi'i 'irfan (Mulla Sadra, Tabataba'i) at all. Nothing represents the critics — no Ibn Taymiyya or Hanbali anti-Sufi polemic, no reformist or modernist objection — so purification is never argued against. Geographically it is Arab-Persian-Turkish only: no Chishti/South Asian, West African, or Southeast Asian Sufism, and no social-historical account of the tariqa as institution (ritual, shaykh-disciple authority, samaa). Women's voices exist only as a to-read scholarly study of Rabi'a, not as texts. Attar appears only as a children's picture-book retelling rather than a full Conference of the Birds, and there is no critical scholarship on how Sufi 'psychology' maps or fails to map onto modern clinical categories.
misfiled: Letters to a Young Poet
Think on These Things
Why You Act the Way You Do
Master of the Jinn

subjects.name: Technique and Attention: The Critique of Technological Society
subjects.description: The tradition that asks not whether a technology works but what it does to human ends — from Ellul and Mumford to attention economies and AI ethics.
subjects.why_this_library: Two Elluls, Mumford, Mander and Postman anchor a lineage that then runs forward into Turkle, Odell, Newport, Han, Finn and Vallor.
subjects.shape: This is a genuinely broad spread across the tradition: the foundational systems critique (Ellul twice, Mumford's Pentagon of Power, Mander's indigenous-alternative counterpoint), the media-ecology strand (Postman, Turkle), the attention-economy literature (Odell, Burkeman, Newport twice, Han's Burnout Society), and a substantial AI-ethics cluster (Vallor, Russell, Christian, Finn). It also carries a contemplative/solitude wing — Merton, Rilke, Busch, McGilchrist — that would let a course frame attention as a spiritual and perceptual capacity rather than just a resource being harvested. The weak spot in commitment rather than coverage: almost everything is to-read, and the only books actually finished are the softest ones (Burkeman, Wenger, a DNF'd Odell).
subjects.holes: No feminist or labor critique of technology — no Ruth Schwartz Cowan, no Shoshana Zuboff on surveillance capitalism, no Astra Taylor or accounts of platform work. The political economy of attention is represented mainly by Wenger, a VC, rather than by anyone analyzing ownership, advertising markets, or regulation. Missing the philosophy-of-technology scholarly tradition after Ellul: no Heidegger's 'Question Concerning Technology', no Borgmann, no Feenberg, no Winner on artifacts and politics — the leap from Mumford to 2020s trade books skips fifty years. Also absent: any pro-technology or techno-optimist interlocutor with real teeth, any history of a specific technology's adoption, any non-Western voice besides Mander's account of indigenous nations (written by an outsider), and empirical psychology of attention rather than argument about it.
misfiled: Mastermind: How to Think Like Sherlock Holmes
Innovation + Equality: How to Create a Future That Is More Star Trek Than Terminator

subjects.name: Trauma, the Body, and the Therapeutic Society
subjects.description: What trauma science claims about bodies and healing, set against critiques of diagnosis, therapy culture, and the globalized psyche.
subjects.why_this_library: Van der Kolk, Levine, Maté and Stanley are shelved with their sharpest opponents — Shrier, Rieff, Watters, Chapman, Insel — making the course an argument, not a treatment plan.
subjects.shape: This is a genuinely two-sided library: the somatic-trauma canon is here in force and fully read (van der Kolk, Levine, Maté twice, Stanley), alongside the wellness-industry primary sources it spawned (Dispenza, Wim Hof) — which makes for a nice unit on how trauma science becomes self-help. Against that sits a real critique wing: Rieff on therapeutic culture replacing moral community, Watters on the export of American diagnostic categories, Chapman's Marxist account of 'normality,' Shrier on overdiagnosis in childhood, Wang on diagnosis and identity. A third strand — Linklater, Duran, DeGruy — reframes trauma as colonial and historical injury rather than individual nervous-system dysregulation, and Freshwater, All Quiet, and The Frightened Ones give literary testimony from Nigerian, WWI German, and Syrian vantage points. Easily six to eight units, though nearly all the critical material is still to-read while the somatic canon is read and five-starred.
subjects.holes: No history or genealogy of the PTSD diagnosis itself — nothing like Ruth Leys, Allan Young, or Hacking on how the category was built through DSM politics and veterans' advocacy. No feminist trauma theory: Judith Herman's Trauma and Recovery is the conspicuous absence, and with it the incest/domestic-violence origins of the modern trauma concept and the memory wars of the 1990s. Nothing empirically skeptical about the specific science the read books assert — no critique of polyvagal theory, ACEs effect sizes, or somatic claims, so Levine and van der Kolk go unchallenged on their own ground while being challenged only culturally. Shrier is the only anti-therapy argument from the read pile and it's popular polemic; there's no defense of global mental health or psychiatric treatment from clinicians (Patel, or a serious psychiatric rebuttal to Watters). Also missing: Freud or any psychoanalytic primary text, despite Rieff and Shaw presupposing one.
misfiled: Fourth Wing (The Empyrean, #1)
Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)
We Were Liars
Milk and honey

subjects.name: Platform Capitalism: Rent, Data, and the New Monopolies
subjects.description: How digital platforms extract value from users, workers, and markets — and what antitrust, labor, and abolitionist responses look like.
subjects.why_this_library: Doctorow, Varoufakis, Srnicek, Larson, Tim Wu, Gray, Noble and two insider tech memoirs let political economy and whistleblower testimony argue with each other.
subjects.shape: This is a well-stocked critique library: the political-economy spine is genuinely there (Srnicek's platform typology, Varoufakis on cloud rent, Larson on monopoly formation, Doctorow on platform decay), and it's flanked by distinct angles rather than repetition — hidden labor (Ghost Work), algorithmic racism (Noble), abolitionist/border tech (Benjamin), techno-solutionism debunking (Broussard), a prehistory of data-driven manipulation (Lepore's If Then), and three insider disillusionment memoirs (McNamee, Wynn-Williams, Liu). Omojuwa adds a rare non-Western, pro-platform-opportunity voice. Notably, almost everything load-bearing is to-read, while what's actually been read skews to journalism and novels — the course exists on the shelf, not yet in the owner's head.
subjects.holes: No antitrust or legal scholarship at all — no Lina Khan, Tim Wu, Teachout, or anything on the actual doctrinal fight over monopoly, essential facilities, or merger review, which the subject description promises. No Zuboff, so surveillance capitalism as a named framework is absent. Labor coverage is one book: nothing on gig-work ethnography or driver algorithmic management (Rosenblat, Dubal), warehouse labor, content moderation work, or platform union organizing. No economics of rent from inside the discipline — no data on take rates, network effects, or market structure, only narrative critique. Geographically it is US-centric: nothing on Chinese platforms, Indian digital public infrastructure, or platform cooperatives and alternative ownership models beyond slogan-level abolitionism. And no serious defense of platforms — no market-liberal or pro-consumer-welfare case to argue against.
misfiled: Catching Fire (The Hunger Games, #2)
When No One Is Watching
This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race

subjects.name: Rereading Scripture: Islamic Feminism and Religious Authority
subjects.description: How women scholars and reformers have contested patriarchal readings of Qur'an, hadith, and law — and how veiling became a global political symbol.
subjects.why_this_library: Wadud, Barlas, Mernissi, Lamrabet, Leila Ahmed, Abou El Fadl, Nadwi and Joan Scott are all here together, so the debate can be staged from inside rather than described from outside.
subjects.shape: This is a genuinely strong core on Qur'anic hermeneutics and religious authority: Wadud, Barlas, and Lamrabet give three distinct egalitarian rereadings of the text, Mernissi supplies the hadith-critical method, and Abou El Fadl supplies the jurisprudential question of who gets to speak in God's name. Around that sits a good second ring — Nadwi's recovery of women hadith transmitters as historical precedent, Schimmel on the feminine in Sufi devotion, De Sondy turning the lens onto masculinity, Rahemtulla situating all of it in liberation theology, and Ahmed plus the Heath anthology carrying the veiling thread as history and symbol rather than polemic. The library even holds its own foils: Manji and Sasson are exactly the reform-polemic and native-informant genres a course would want to put on the table and interrogate.
subjects.holes: The biggest gap is the scholarly critique of Islamic feminism from within — Kecia Ali's argument that Qur'anic egalitarianism can't be squared with classical fiqh on marriage and slavery, and Saba Mahmood's ethnographic challenge to the liberal agency assumptions underlying the whole project. Lila Abu-Lughod on rescue narratives is missing precisely where you'd want it, next to Manji and Sasson. There is no legal-reform-in-practice material (Mir-Hosseini, Musawah, personal status code campaigns), no Shi'i or Iranian voice, and nothing from Southeast Asia or West Africa — the geography is Arab world plus North America plus one Danish mosque. Colonial-era origins of the veil debate (Qasim Amin, Sha'rawi, Ahmed's earlier Women and Gender in Islam) are absent, so the veiling unit starts mid-story. Finally there are no primary sources: no tafsir excerpt, no hadith collection, no classical fiqh text, so students would only ever meet the patriarchal tradition through its critics' summaries. A traditionalist defending complementarity in her own voice would sharpen every week.
misfiled: All About Love: New Visions
Kaikeyi
Morgan Is My Name (Morgan le Fay, #1)
Mexican Gothic
Who Cooked the Last Supper? The Women's History of the World
The Vegetarian
When Women Ruled the World: Six Queens of Egypt
A Woman Is No Man

subjects.name: Abolition as Method: Policing, Prisons, and Transformative Justice
subjects.description: The abolitionist tradition as analysis and practice — policing, carceral feminism, community accountability, and the funding of activism itself.
subjects.why_this_library: Vitale, Kaba, Gilmore, Davis, Dixon, Thuma, Benjamin and INCITE! are here in enough depth to cover strategy and internal critique, not just slogans.
subjects.shape: This is a genuinely multi-stranded abolitionist library: a policing critique (Vitale), the movement's canonical organizing texts (Kaba, Gilmore, Davis), a practice-oriented transformative justice anthology (Dixon), a movement history of carceral feminism (Thuma), a self-critique of movement infrastructure (INCITE!'s Revolution Will Not Be Funded), a prison memoir (Assata), and adjacent strands on surveillance/borders (Benjamin) and Indigenous decolonial struggle (Red Deal). brown and Spade supply the interior, relational side of the practice — how movements and intimate lives are organized — and Snyder's domestic violence reporting is the one non-abolitionist voice that can be read against the carceral-feminism unit. Weeks build easily: critique of policing, racial capitalism, carceral feminism, TJ practice, funding and co-optation, prison writing, borders and tech.
subjects.holes: Almost no scholarly history of how the carceral state was built — nothing like Hinton, Muhammad, Gottschalk, or Blackmon on convict leasing, so the 'why prisons exist' unit rests on essays rather than archives. No penological or philosophical theory of punishment (Foucault, Davis's own Are Prisons Obsolete?, retributivist or reformist philosophers), and no serious interlocutor who thinks reform or policing can work — the course would never encounter its strongest opponent. Courts, prosecution, bail, sentencing and parole are entirely absent: the pipeline is discussed only at its policing and prison ends. Also missing: any empirical evaluation of community accountability or restorative programs (does TJ work, and by what measure), survivor voices that resist abolitionist framing beyond Snyder, and comparative/international carceral material outside the Palestine and India gestures. Field Notes on Democracy and Born in Flames sit loosely at the edges — usable as state-violence and urban-disinvestment context, but neither is an abolition text.
misfiled: Sunrise on the Reaping (The Hunger Games)

subjects.name: Knowledge Under Empire: Whose Science, Whose Reason?
subjects.description: Six weeks on how knowledge gets made, transmitted, and ranked — from the Greek-Arabic translation movement to decolonial epistemology and the sociology of laboratories.
subjects.why_this_library: It pairs the Islamic history-of-science shelf (Saliba, Dallal, Bakar, Freely) with Feyerabend, Knorr Cetina, Mignolo, Chakrabarty and Hallaq — a genuinely rare combination.
subjects.shape: This library's version of the subject is heavily weighted toward the Islamic and postcolonial critique of Western knowledge: transmission history (Freely, Saliba, Dallal), Islamic classification and epistemology (Bakar, al-Attas, Hallaq on Taha Abdurrahman), and decolonial/postcolonial theory (Mignolo, Chakrabarty, Hallaq's Restating Orientalism). Ogunnaike adds a genuinely comparative West African dimension, and Knorr Cetina supplies the one real laboratory-ethnography anchor, with Feyerabend providing an internal Western attack on scientific authority. It could plausibly run six weeks: Greek-Arabic transmission, Islamic classification of the sciences, science-and-religion in Islamic history, coloniality and Orientalism, alternative epistemologies, and the sociology of science.
subjects.holes: The sociology-of-knowledge week rests on a single book — no Latour, Shapin and Schaffer, Bloor, Daston, or Haraway, so laboratory studies and feminist standpoint epistemology are nearly absent. There is no Said himself, despite two books that argue with him, and no defenders of universalist science or rationalism to argue against (no Sokal-style rebuttal, no philosophy-of-science mainstream). Chinese, Indian, and indigenous American knowledge traditions are missing entirely, as is the colonial-science-in-practice literature (botany, surveying, medicine under empire — Schiebinger, Raj, Prakash). Guenon's traditionalism sits in as metaphysics rather than as a studied object, with no critical framing of the perennialist position itself.
misfiled: Aladdin: A New Translation
A Critical History and Philosophy of Psychology: Diversity of Context, Thought, and Practice

subjects.name: After Growth: Degrowth, Ecosocialism, and Climate Politics
subjects.description: The anti-growth turn in ecological thought, from degrowth economics and ecofeminism to sabotage, indigenous critique, and climate justice.
subjects.why_this_library: Saitō, Hickel, Löwy, Raworth, Shiva, Malm and Ghosh sit beside Haraway and Fresh Banana Leaves, so the economics is constantly interrupted by cosmology and tactics.
subjects.shape: This is a genuinely multi-voiced anti-growth library: degrowth economics (Hickel, Saitō, Raworth), ecosocialism (Löwy), militant tactics (Malm), ecofeminism (Shiva/Mies), indigenous and decolonial critique (The Red Deal, Fresh Banana Leaves, Ghosh's Nutmeg's Curse), multispecies posthumanism (Haraway), and an unusual religious-traditionalist strand (Nasr, Helminski) that most reading lists on this topic omit entirely. Thunberg's anthology gives a broad factual and activist baseline to anchor the more polemical texts. The arguments actually disagree with each other — Malm's sabotage against Nasr's spiritual recovery, Saitō's degrowth communism against Raworth's reformist doughnut — which is what makes six to eight distinct units possible.
subjects.holes: There is no serious opposition. Nothing here defends growth: no ecomodernism (Bastani, Phillips, Symons), no mainstream climate economics (Nordhaus, Stern, Weitzman), no energy-systems realism (Smil, Vaclav-style materials and scale constraints). The left-internal critique of degrowth as austerity-for-the-poor or as unworkable for the Global South is absent, as is any Global South developmentalist voice arguing that growth is precisely what's owed. The intellectual prehistory is missing — Limits to Growth, Schumacher, Georgescu-Roegen, Illich — so degrowth appears as a 2020s invention rather than a fifty-year tradition. Also no concrete policy or institutional material: Green New Deal legislation, just-transition labor politics, or any account of what a degrowth state would actually do about pensions, debt, and employment. Finally, all but four books are unread, so the course rests on assumed rather than tested material.
misfiled: The Hidden Life of Trees: What They Feel, How They Communicate: Discoveries from a Secret World
Beyond the Periphery of the Skin: Rethinking, Remaking, and Reclaiming the Body in Contemporary Capitalism (Kairos)

subjects.name: Reading the City: Gentrification, Design, and the Right to Stay
subjects.description: Why neighbourhoods get emptied, burned, financed, and redesigned — and what humane density and social infrastructure would require instead.
subjects.why_this_library: Jacobs, Speck, Sim and Hajer on design sit next to Moskowitz, Ansfield, Horn and a gentrification thriller — the aesthetic and the extractive read together.
subjects.shape: This is a library with genuinely distinct angles on the same city block: the extraction mechanics (Ansfield on landlord arson, Horn on East New York mortgage fraud, Moskowitz's four-city reporting), the design canon (Jacobs, Speck, Sim, Montgomery), and the collective-goods case (Klinenberg on libraries and pools, Hajer on the neighbourhood as ecological unit, Sheller on who gets to move). It could plausibly run as: how neighborhoods were destroyed on purpose → how they get repriced → what good density looks like → what shared space does → mobility as a right. Cole's thriller gives the whole thing a resident's-eye entry point, and it's the one book actually read.
subjects.holes: No political economy of rent and real estate capital — no Neil Smith's rent gap, no Harvey, nothing on REITs, private equity landlords, or how capital actually decides which block is next, which leaves the 'financed' part of the premise underserved. No state racial policy: no redlining/FHA history (Rothstein-type), no public housing history, no urban renewal from the displaced side. The 'right to stay' has no organizing literature at all — no tenant unions, rent control, community land trusts, eviction ethnography (Desmond and similar are absent), so the course can diagnose but not act. Geographically it is US plus Copenhagen/Dutch design; nothing on Global South urbanism, informal settlements, colonial land regimes, or Indigenous claims to urban land. Zoning and the supply-side/YIMBY argument never gets a defender, so Jacobs-style density goes unchallenged. And almost everything is unread, so the sequencing is aspirational rather than tested.
misfiled: Against Creativity

subjects.name: Ink and Sand: Islam and Scholarship in West Africa
subjects.description: The intellectual, spiritual, and political history of Muslim West Africa, from manuscript libraries and embodied Qur'anic pedagogy to Sufi resistance under colonial rule.
subjects.why_this_library: Ware (twice), Kane, Babou, Kimball, Ogunnaike, Diouf and Ibn Battuta form a coherent syllabus on a region usually reduced to a footnote in Islamic studies.
subjects.shape: This is a Senegal-weighted, Sufi-centered version of the subject with a genuine spine: Ware's two volumes give you both the embodied-pedagogy argument about Qur'anic schooling and a translated anthology of West African Sufi writing, so you have primary texts as well as interpretation. Kane supplies the long survey from Timbuktu's manuscripts to modern Muslim intellectual life, Ibn Battuta anchors the medieval Sahelian end, and Kimball plus Babou give you devotional and scholarly accounts of the same figure (Amadu Bamba) under French rule — a useful paired reading on hagiography versus archival history. Ogunnaike adds the one genuinely comparative unit, putting Sufi knowledge alongside Ifá as rival epistemologies.
subjects.holes: The eastern and Hausa side of Muslim West Africa is absent: nothing on the Sokoto Caliphate, Usman dan Fodio's own treatises, the nineteenth-century jihad states, or Nigeria at all. The Timbuktu manuscript tradition is invoked by title but never read directly — no Ahmad Baba, no Tarikh al-Sudan or Tarikh al-Fattash, no codicology or the Ahmed Baba Institute's preservation politics. Also missing: the Suwarian/Mande tradition of accommodation (Sanneh), the Tijaniyya as an order distinct from the Muridiyya, twentieth-century Salafi and Izala reformism against Sufism, the Islamic debates over slavery and enslavement of Muslims that Ware only gestures at, women's learning within West Africa specifically (Al-Muhaddithat is pan-Islamic and does no African work), and contemporary ethnography of Murid labor, migration, and Touba's economy. Four of the six load-bearing books are unread, so the course as taught currently rests on Ware plus a hagiography.
misfiled: Neo-traditionalism in Islam in the West: Orthodoxy, Spirituality and Politics
The Rise of Humanism in Classical Islam and the Christian West

subjects.name: Why Civilizations Come Apart
subjects.description: Competing explanations of societal breakdown — elite overproduction, plague and climate, environmental mismanagement, and violence as the great leveller.
subjects.why_this_library: Three Turchin volumes plus Toynbee, Scheidel, Harper, Rosen and two Diamonds turn a vague anxiety into a genuine methodological argument.
subjects.shape: Seven serious nonfiction titles, each carrying a different causal engine: Turchin's structural-demographic modeling (twice, with Ages of Discord extending it to modern America), Diamond on environmental self-destruction, Harper and Rosen on climate and pandemic in Rome and Byzantium, Scheidel on violence as the only real leveller of inequality, and Toynbee as the older grand-pattern tradition against which all of these are reactions. The late-antique Mediterranean is the best-covered case by far — you could run two weeks on Rome's end alone using Harper and Rosen together. The shape is breadth of thesis rather than depth on any one: one book per explanation, arranged as a debate.
subjects.holes: No skeptics or deflators — nothing arguing that 'collapse' is a category error, that societies transform rather than fall (Tainter's diminishing-returns account, Middleton, the resilience/archaeology-of-continuity literature, or the critiques of Diamond's Easter Island and Norse chapters that every seminar on Collapse needs). No pre-classical or non-Western collapse cases in their own right: Bronze Age Mediterranean, Maya, Angkor, Harappa, the Han and Ming transitions appear only as Diamond vignettes or Toynbee abstractions. No primary sources at all — no Procopius, no chronicles of the Black Death, no contemporary voices from inside a breakdown. Also missing the state-capacity and institutional-economics angle (Acemoglu/Robinson, Scott on the grain state) and any serious treatment of Turchin's methodological critics, which matters when two of nine books are his.
misfiled: Between Two Fires
All the Birds in the Sky

subjects.name: Palestine in Prose, Poetry, and Testimony
subjects.description: Diaries, novels, poems, and polemics on siege, erasure, exile, and the problem of representing occupation.
subjects.why_this_library: Abu Saif, Azem, Zaher, Abulhawa, Kanazi, Peled and Davis together move between speculative fiction, war diary, verse and abolitionist solidarity.
subjects.shape: The genuinely Palestinian core is small but well-chosen: Kanazi's spoken-word poems, Azem's The Book of Disappearance as a formal experiment in erasure, Zaher's The Coin as diaspora unease, plus three unread anchors (Abulhawa's prison-cell novel, Abu Saif's Gaza diary, Peled's Israeli defector memoir) and Angela Davis's Ferguson–Palestine solidarity speeches. What's actually read is four books, two of them contemporary diaspora fiction, which makes this a strong seminar on Palestinian writing *now* — voice, vanishing, and the anglophone diaspora novel — rather than a course. Around it sits a large ring of adjacent occupation and exile literature (Iraq, Afghanistan, Iran, Algeria, refugee fiction) that reads as a comparative impulse never organized into one.
subjects.holes: No Palestinian canon: no Darwish, no Kanafani, no Emile Habibi, no Mourid Barghouti, no Adania Shibli — so the poetry unit rests on one contemporary voice and the 'problem of representing occupation' has no Said (neither Orientalism, The Question of Palestine, nor Out of Place). Nothing from before 1990: no Nakba testimony, no oral history from the camps, no 1948 or First Intifada material, so 'erasure' is asserted rather than documented. No historiography or polemic proper (Khalidi, Pappé, Masalha), no Israeli or Zionist argument to read against except one defector memoir, no reportage or graphic testimony from Gaza beyond a single unread diary, and no Palestinian women's or peasant oral testimony. Half the Palestine shelf is unread, including the two nonfiction testimonies a course would build weeks on.

subjects.name: Indigenous Knowledge, Healing, and Land
subjects.description: Indigenous epistemologies and healing practices as intellectual traditions, and what colonization did to land, medicine, and memory.
subjects.why_this_library: Four Mehl-Madrona titles plus Linklater, Duran, Hernandez, Yunkaporta, Charleston, Black Elk and The Red Deal make healing, not just history, the centre of gravity.
subjects.shape: This is really a clinical-healing library with a thin historical frame attached. Four of the twelve books are by Lewis Mehl-Madrona making substantially the same argument \u2014 that story and ceremony belong inside medicine \u2014 and Duran and Linklater extend the same therapeutic frame into intergenerational trauma, so roughly half the collection converges on Indigenous healing as a corrective to Western psychotherapy. Everything else is one book deep: one settler-colonial history (Dunbar-Ortiz), one land/conservation title (Hernandez), one epistemology text (Sand Talk), one mediated elder narrative (Black Elk Speaks, the only book read). The 'land' half of the subject title is carried almost entirely by Hernandez and Mander, the latter a non-Indigenous technology critic.
subjects.holes: No Indigenous research methodology or epistemology scholarship \u2014 no Linda Tuhiwai Smith, no Vine Deloria Jr., no Kimmerer-style science-and-ceremony work to give Sand Talk company. Nothing on law and dispossession as mechanism: treaties, allotment, Indian Claims Commission, land-back organizing, water and pipeline struggles. No residential/boarding school record from within \u2014 no survivor testimony, no Truth and Reconciliation Commission material \u2014 which leaves the trauma books asserting a history the library never documents. No nation-specific depth: the collection moves from Lakota to Cherokee to Anishinaabe to Yolngu to Latin America without ever staying long enough to show how knowledge is held by a particular people in a particular place. Black Elk Speaks is present without any of the scholarship on Neihardt's mediation, so the problem of the white transcriber goes unexamined. Also missing: contemporary Indigenous poetry, fiction, or essay that isn't framed as therapy, and any skeptical or internal-critique voice on the healing claims in the Coyote books.
misfiled: Blood at the Root: A Racial Cleansing in America

subjects.name: Scheherazade's Inheritance: Arabic Storytelling and Its Modern Retellings
subjects.description: The Nights, the Arabic epic, and the jinn tradition — plus the contemporary fantasy and criticism that rewrite them.
subjects.why_this_library: Kilito's criticism, a new Aladdin, the Princess Fatima epic and Chakraborty/Abdullah/Karchmar novels let theory and pulp be taught in the same week.
subjects.shape: This is mostly a contemporary-fantasy shelf with a few classical anchors bolted on: three read Anglophone novels drawing on jinn and Arabian folklore (Abdullah, Chakraborty x2), plus Byatt's djinn novella, sitting beside a single translated Nights tale (Horta's Aladdin), one translated Arabic epic (Dhat al-Himma), and Kilito's essays on how classical Arabic culture thought about narrative. The Orientalism critique corner (Hallaq, Arjana) gives a reception/appropriation angle. Nearly all the non-fiction and translation is unread, so the lived strength is the modern retelling side — the library knows what the Nights became in 2020s fantasy far better than what they were.
subjects.holes: There is no Thousand and One Nights — no Haddawy, Lyons, Burton, or Mahdi edition — so the frame tale, Shahrazad herself, and the cycle structure the course is named for exist only by rumor. No scholarship on the Nights' textual history or its European fabrication (Horta's own Marvellous Thieves, Irwin's Companion, Naddaff on the frame). No jinn scholarship (El-Zein) to ground the tradition the novels borrow from. No Said's Orientalism, only two books arguing past it. Nothing from the Arabic-language modern side — Mahfouz's Arabian Nights and Days, Haidar, Djebar — so 'modern retellings' means Anglophone retellings only. No sira literature beyond the one Dhat al-Himma selection, no Persian or Indian antecedents, no oral-performance or hakawati material.
misfiled: Wolfish: Wolf, Self, and the Stories We Tell About Fear
Women Who Run With the Wolves

subjects.name: The Politics of the Terraces: Football, Power, and the Crowd
subjects.description: Football as a laboratory for nationalism, dictatorship, commercialization, and organized fan resistance.
subjects.why_this_library: Four books by four authors — Montague, Kuhn, Kuper, Foer — give a full spectrum from ultras ethnography to anarchist fan politics, which is an unusual shelf to own.
subjects.shape: What's actually here is four books of globe-trotting journalism on football and politics — Foer, Kuper, Montague, Kuhn — three of which share nearly identical premises (a reporter travels the world using clubs and fan cultures to explain nationalism, ethnic conflict and power). The strongest distinct contribution is Kuhn on radical left football culture and Montague on ultras as an organized subculture. Only one of the four has been read, and the owner rated it 2 stars.
subjects.holes: No academic or sociological treatment of crowds and fandom (no Armstrong, Giulianotti, or stadium-disaster and policing literature like Hillsborough). No single-country deep history — nothing on Franco's Barcelona, Mussolini's Italy, Argentina's junta, or apartheid South Africa as sustained case studies rather than travelogue chapters. Nothing on the political economy of commercialization: TV rights, oligarch and state ownership, sportswashing, Qatar and the World Cup labor question. No women's football or gender politics of the terraces, no fan-ownership/protest movements told from inside (e.g. against the Super League), and no primary sources — fanzine writing, supporter-group manifestos, club documents. Also entirely Anglophone-journalist perspective; no translated or scholarly voices from the countries described.

subjects.name: Who Owns the Past? Archaeology, Heritage, and Nationalism
subjects.description: How digs, museums, and world-heritage bureaucracies turned antiquity into political property across Egypt, Iraq, and the colonial metropole.
subjects.why_this_library: Two Meskell books plus Bernhardsson, Fagan, Procter, Al-Rashid and even Christie's dig mystery make the politics of excavation a subject rather than a sidebar.
subjects.shape: Too few books in this library to judge.
